facts.text: Wabi refers to a simple, understated and austere kind of beauty.
Sabi refers to the beauty of things that have aged well or gained a worn surface; another Japanese word pronounced sabi means rust.
The combined term wabi-sabi joins two related ideas, often linked with humble, lonely or melancholy feelings, and together they suggest a plain, unpretentious country style.

In Essays in Idleness, written in 1332, the Buddhist priest Yoshida Kenkō asked whether people should look at cherry blossoms only when they are in full bloom, or at the moon only when the sky is clear.
Kenkō wrote that branches about to blossom and gardens covered with faded flowers deserve even more admiration.
The idea of wabi was first praised in poetry, but it was developed most fully in the art of tea.
The tea master Sen no Rikyū (1522–1591) created a style of tea gathering known as wabicha.
Rikyū opposed the fashion for importing expensive tea ware from China and preferred objects made locally.
Rikyū asked a local potter, Chōjirō, to make tea bowls in a new style, Raku ware: rough earthenware that was plain, often uneven and imperfect in shape and finish, unlike refined Chinese porcelain.
Raku firing and drying methods allowed heat, air and gravity to leave their own marks on the clay.
A 1690 record of Rikyū’s teachings advises that the utensils in a small tea room should be less than adequate, and says that disliking a piece because of slight damage shows a lack of understanding.
In the wabi taste, utensils with small flaws were often valued more highly than perfect ones, and broken pieces that had been well repaired more highly than unbroken ones.
The wabi taste means moderation rather than extreme self-denial; a meal for a small tea gathering, for example, should be one soup and two or three dishes.
The garden of Saihōji temple in Kyoto was designed in 1339 by the priest and master gardener Musō Soseki.
When the garden was first made, it was a landscape of white sand and green pine trees, also known for its cherry blossoms; it was not covered in moss.
The moss built up gradually over time, especially during the Edo period (1603–1868), when the temple fell into disrepair.
One theory says that after repeated floods, mud dredged from the pond was piled on its islands, and moss later grew on that mud.
Today more than 120 kinds of moss cover the grounds, and the temple is widely known as Kokedera, the moss temple.
In winter the grounds are swept as little as possible so that the resting moss is not disturbed.
Leonard Koren’s book on wabi-sabi for artists, designers, poets and philosophers first appeared in 1994, and the term has since been gaining currency outside Japan.
